questions.question: A worker may crash during a multi-hour agent run. What infrastructure lets another worker resume the run's saved progress?
options: A round-robin selector over every registered agent
A longer system prompt copied into each worker
An in-memory queue that disappears with the process
Durable checkpoints keyed by the run identifier
questions.explanation: A durable checkpoint keyed by run identifier stores serializable progress so another worker can resume after a crash. An in-memory queue disappears with its process and cannot reconstruct the workflow state.

questions.question: What three-state lifecycle does the lesson's per-agent queue use?
options: Submitted, Working, Completed
Open, Closed, Half-Open
Idle, Processing, Response
Propose, Accept, Verify
questions.explanation: The per-agent queue cycles through Idle, Processing, and Response as it accepts, handles, and emits a message. Open, Closed, and Half-Open describe a circuit breaker, not this producer-consumer lifecycle.

questions.question: Why is async I/O useful for many concurrent LLM calls?
options: Waiting calls can yield instead of occupying one thread each
It removes the need to store workflow state
It guarantees the remote provider returns tokens faster
It makes CPU-bound parsing execute without any processor time
questions.explanation: Async tasks yield while network calls wait for tokens, allowing the event loop to advance other waiting calls. This improves concurrency for I/O-bound work, but it does not make the remote provider generate tokens faster.

questions.question: What is Bedi's pragmatic counterpoint to adopting a durable workflow engine too early?
options: Start with FastAPI and Postgres until measured load requires more
Avoid databases and store every run in process memory
Adopt every queue and checkpoint system before launch
Use a distributed actor framework for every prototype
questions.explanation: Bedi’s counterpoint is to begin with FastAPI plus Postgres and adopt a heavier workflow engine when measured load or state needs justify it. Installing every queue and checkpoint system before a demonstrated need adds ceremony without evidence of benefit.

questions.question: A queue may deliver a payment task more than once. What makes the effect effectively once?
options: At-least-once delivery paired with a deduplication key
A retry that creates a fresh payment key each time
An async worker that suppresses every second request
Exactly-once delivery assumed without recording identifiers
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery may repeat a message, so use the same stable deduplication key and an idempotent consumer that honors it; retries then create one effective side effect. Creating a fresh key for every retry defeats deduplication.

questions.question: Long-running agents may remain active during a software deploy. What rollout pattern reduces disruption?
options: Terminate every active run and restart from the first task
Route every checkpoint to the newest code immediately
Keep multiple runtime versions live while older runs drain
Disable checkpoints until the deployment finishes
questions.explanation: Rainbow deployment keeps older runtime versions available until their in-flight stateful runs drain, while new runs can move gradually to the new version. Immediate restart risks interrupting saved work or changing the code that resumes it.
